lede: MinAtar's Breakout with one change: the players see a single frame, so nothing on screen says which way the ball is moving. Cadence 0.89.0 added a way for its recall memory to look things up by when they happened, which sounds like exactly the missing piece. Over 12 seeds, the new position term did not make the shipped memory play better ({wins} seeds better, {losses} worse). It did fully stand in for the memory's built-in recency nudge when that was switched off (better in all {rwins} seeds). And the best Cadence player here used no recall memory at all.
replaynote: Showcase: seed {seed}, the median seed of the position-term brain by score, so a typical one. All six boards are the same test game (same serve, same sticky-action luck until the players' moves diverge), played with no coaching. The percentage is how often the player's move matched what the coach would have said.
curvecap: Median bricks per test game (3 games per test, at most 300 moments each) after each 1,000 training moments, 12 seeds per player. The shaded window is the last {last} tests, which the headline numbers average. The two-frame MLP (dashed) is a reference: it is handed where the ball was, which the others have to remember.
verdict: As shipped, no. With the founder memory, the brain with the position term scored {pos32} bricks per game and the same brain built with recall_position=0 scored {pos0}. That is a coin flip across seeds. The founder memory already prefers recent moments with a fixed recency nudge, and in this game "the moment just before" is all that matters, so the learned term had nothing to add. With the nudge turned off (recall_recency=0, the setting of upstream's look-back benchmark), the term learned to do that job by itself: {r32} vs {r0} bricks, better in all {rwins} seeds, ending about where the founder memory does. The surprise is the third Cadence arm: with no recall memory at all the brain scored {norecall}, more than the position-term brain in 8 of 12 seeds and more than the plain-recall brain in 11 of 12, and about as much as the MLP that is handed two frames ({mlp2}). Cadence's own settle carries the moment before into the next one, and here that was enough to read the ball's direction.
paircap: Each dot is one seed: bricks per game with the position term minus without it, averaged over the last {last} tests. Bar: median. Red dots favour the term, blue dots favour the memory without it.
tblcap: Last {last} tests, median over 12 seeds (seeds 10–21). The two "recency off" rows are the second, pre-declared condition. Random play scores {random}.
limits: The position term learns only from taught lessons, never from rewards. So this demo teaches every moment with a coach. Played for points alone through Brain.live, the term never moves, and brains with and without it chose the same 5,000 actions on two seeds (checked, identity.py).

One game, one small brain (one 32-neuron module), 30,000 training moments, 12 seeds. Settings were picked on pilot seeds 0–2, which aren't reported. Predictions and metrics were written into run.py and committed before the main run.

Pre-declared predictions: P1 (term beats founder memory) failed; P2 (recall at least matches no recall) failed, recall was worse; P3 (two frames beat one for the MLP, 12 of 12) and P4 (all beat random) held; P5 (term beats no term with recency off, 12 of 12) held.

This order question is the shortest one there is: one moment back. Upstream's look-back benchmark asks for the first of five, which recency cannot answer. A game that needs "what happened at the start" would test the term harder.
The players see 49 hand-made numbers (ball column, row, paddle column, their difference), not pixels. The coach is perfect and never loses a ball. Scores are capped by the 300-moment test games.
A replay of recorded games. The brains learned in Python on a desktop CPU, not in your browser.
foot: MinAtar Breakout: Kenny Young and Tian Tian, "MinAtar: An Atari-inspired Testbed for Thorough and Reproducible Reinforcement Learning Experiments" (2019), GPL-3.0. Cadence: Pragma Research.
